newsitem.title: UK: UK SFA's new executive responsibility rules stall.
newsitem.headline: UK SFA's new executive responsibility rules stall.

text.p: Plans by Britain's Securities and Futures Authority (SFA) to make top executives more responsible stalled on Tuesday as the watchdog said it had to wait for others to catch up.

The SFA said it would not publish the controversial changes to its rules until it was clear they were in line with standards being proposed for the industry as a whole by Britain's top financial regulator Securities and Investments Board.
"We are mindful that our proposals have industry-wide consequences beyond our own regulated firms," the SFA said in a statement.

The SFA, a self-regulating body charged with policing the activities of individuals working in the securities and futures business, said it would not continue until the SIB's work was Together with the SIB it had agreed "there should be no further SFA consultation until the SIB's own work has reached a more advanced stage", adding it would not issue its proposals until it knew there were "in harmony with the SIB's standards".

The SFA received more than 100 responses to its consultation paper which suggested that the burden of proof in the event of a firm suffering catastrophic failure should fall on senior management rather than the regulator.
Current regulations, although they assign ultimate responsibility to top executives, are thought too vague to be sufficiently effective.
The new rules have been drawn up since the former Barings chairman Peter Baring and his deputy Andrew Tuckey escaped prosecution under SFA rules.

At the time the proposals were announced, the SFA said management structure at Barings, which collapsed in February 1995, had not worked, although it had a matrix management and internal control structure typical of internationally active investment firms.
Responses to the plans, many of which were hostile, came from industry trade groups, regulated firms and others and were considered by two committees of its board and the board itself.

After the SFA's consultation was launched in September last year, the SIB announced its own initiative to examine senior management responsibility in October. As a result the SFA will now make its findings from the consultation and the board's deliberations available to the SIB "and will continue to stress the responsibility of senior management for the control and compliance environment of their firms".
